subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MISSION TO SOVIET UNION AND VISIT TO YUGOSLAVIA

speakeroldname: Hon. Alasiair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MISSION TO SOVIET UNION AND VISIT TO YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a brief statement about the mission which I led to the U.S.S.R. between October 14 and 19 in connection with the Third Mixed Commission under our intergovernmental agreement on co-operation in the industrial application of science and technology. In addition, I would also like to report that after the mission to Moscow I visited Belgrade to sign the first bilateral trade agreement between Canada and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.
During my stay in Belgrade I had discussions with a number of senior Yugoslavian officials, including Prime Minister Bijedich, Dr. Vratusha, Vice-President of the Federal Executive Council, and Dr. Ludwiger, the trade minister, on a wide range of questions affecting trade and economic relations between our two countries. Yugoslavia has become a promising market for Canadian manufactured goods and I look forward to further growth in this trade in the future.
These visits are part of a pattern to seek out new and promising trading opportunities for Canadian exporters.
Accompanying me on my visit to the U.S.S.R. were 36 senior Canadian industrialists representing a large number of companies. This is by far the largest delegation of businessmen a Canadian minister has led to the Soviet Union. This initiative on the part of the Canadian government highlights the business thrust of the activities which have been taking place under our agreement with the Soviet Union.
During the visit, Canadian businessmen associated with the eight working groups set up under the intergovernmental agreement held a large number of meetings, over 80, with their Soviet counterparts. We concluded, as page 4 of the protocol makes clear, that there were a number of important specific opportunities already under negotiation that should be continued and, indeed, some of the businessmen of the delegation remained in Moscow to carry out this work. There was a general consensus among the members of the delegation that the work of our mission represented an important step forward in Canada-Soviet trade and economic relations.
The Soviet Union is becoming an increasingly important market for high technology machinery and equipment
from western countries. I am convinced that there are significant opportunities for Canadian manufacturers to compete for this business. My department has been making vigorous efforts to ensure that Canadian exporters are placed in the best possible position to take advantage of these opportunities.
In addition to my discussions with L. N. Efremov, First Deputy Chairman of the State Committee for Science and Technology, who led the Soviet delegation to the third meeting of the Mixed Commission, I had the opportunity to meet with the First Deputy Chairman of the Council of Ministers, K. T. Mazurov, and other Soviet ministers and senior officials. In these discussions we agreed that there is substantial scope for expanding and diversifying Canada-Soviet trade.
Pursuant to Standing Order 41(2) I should like to place on the table of the House, in both official languages, the protocol which I signed on behalf of the Canadian government on Friday, October 19.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MISSION TO SOVIET UNION AND VISIT TO YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MISSION TO SOVIET UNION AND VISIT TO YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House is pleased to see the minister back safely and to note the additional groundwork undertaken by him in anticipation of increased trade with the Soviet Union.
We read in an Associated Press despatch from Moscow that although the minister felt solid progress had been made in the talks, a breakthrough had yet to occur. The minister is reported to have said: "It is like building a house. You have to clear the site, design the building and lay a foundation. Perhaps not much shows, but a lot of solid work has been done. The test will be to see what appears above ground in the next two or three years." Like the minister, we shall watch the results with great interest and anticipation.
We note, also, that the minister visited Yugoslavia. We hope he managed to visit Dubrovnik for a couple of days, a favourite spot of many people who travel to that part of the world. Yugoslavia offers interesting possibilities for expanded trade. As a matter of fact, it is possible that the rate of expansion of trade with Yugoslavia may be even greater than with the Soviet Union. This is partially, at least, attributable to the fact that the Yugoslavs have been turning more in the direction of personal initiative, including some private enterprise.
The minister tells us his visit was part of a pattern. We welcome the pattern to the extent that the minister, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and other members of the government visit countries abroad with the idea of establishing better relationships and developing opportunities for trade. We would hope, however, that in doing so the minister and the Prime Minister will not neglect those

areas of the world which have traditionally been our major trading partners, in particular, the United States, Britain, Japan, the European Community, and now the Pacific rim countries and South America which offer a tremendous potential to Canadians.
So we hope that in the dying weeks of the present administration-

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MISSION TO SOVIET UNION AND VISIT TO YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the minister back from his visit to the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia.
I join with the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) in expressing hope that the contacts that have been made so far will soon lead to concrete contractual relationships in terms of orders for goods from our country by the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia. In turn, of course, it is anticipated that such orders would be reciprocated by Canadian orders for goods to be supplied by those countries. The talks are making progress, the minister informs us, but up to this point we have not seen concrete results on either side. I certainly hope we shall see them soon.
There is one problem to which no reference was made either in the minister's statement or in the protocol tabled by the minister, probably for understandable reasons. I refer to the problem of foreign ownership of so much of the sophisticated industrial plant located in this country in relation to making sales to either the Soviet Union or Yugoslavia. It would be interesting to know what proportion of the businessmen who accompanied the minister on this trip were, in fact, representatives of United States-owned or other foreign-owned companies in Canada. It seems to me that if there were a substantial number the results of this trip would not necessarily be of benefit to this country.
We have seen the development of a good rapprochement
between the U.S.S.R. and the United States, a cooling down of the high level of heat in terms of the tension that existed between these two countries in the past, with increasing trade talks between them. Therefore the conclusion seems to be rather ominous for us in terms of increasing trade in the precise areas regarding which the minister says the Soviet Union may require exports from the west. Why should Canadian subsidiaries of American companies expect to get orders from the Soviet Union? It seems to me much more likely that United States parent firms of Canadian subsidiaries, either through offering lower prices or by other means, will make sure that contracts go to the United States. This illustrates there is a need to move much more rapidly than the government has indicated it is prepared to in order to regain a greater degree of control over our own industry, particularly advanced, technologically sophisticated industry.

I welcome the minister's return from his attempts to expand trade with the Soviet bloc countries. In welcoming this initiative I should like the minister to note that since he was away we have increased our deficit with our major trading partner, the United States, in automotive products this year for the first time in three years. The size of this deficit would make look like peanuts by comparison any sales we might obtain from the Soviet Union in the near future. Now that the minister has returned I hope he will come to grips with improving our trading relationship with the United States.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MISSION TO SOVIET UNION AND VISIT TO YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister for his trip in the Soviet Union aimed at promoting mutual understanding between our countries and I should like to tell him how hopeful we are for the success of these meetings since, in looking at the terms of agreement that we have been given, we note that these agreements are aimed at advertising Canada and Canadian products. This shows in my opinion that Canada is becoming more mature because instead of exporting only our raw materials to one or two countries like we used to do, we are now proving to other countries that we can profit from technological advances.
As for the meeting with Yugoslavian representatives, we are told that this country has become a promising market for Canadian products. I therefore believe that the time has come for Canada to export manufactured products. If we want Canada to develop, we must stop exporting regularly all our raw materials so that other countries may benefit from them. We are able to manufacture our own products from raw materials here in Canada and we have proved that we are able to export them.
The minister said that he was accompanied by more than 36 Canadian industrialists. I hope that there are many true Canadian industrialists. I am thinking here of the regional industrialists. As everyone knows, in my region we manufacture the biggest slasher-trimmer in the world and we export it all over the world.
I believe that the time has now come for the minister to promote the manufacture of Canadian products.
I therefore congratulate the minister and encourage him in his efforts to conquer world markets.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED AIRPORT-SURVEY OF BIRD FLYWAYS
speechtext: What was the nature of the survey related to the proposed airport in Pickering that required government employees to count birds flying past the moon (a) how long did the employees take to count such birds (b) what was the cost to the government (c) what was the result?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED AIRPORT-SURVEY OF BIRD FLYWAYS
speechtext:
After the announcement of the site for the New Toronto International Airport, certain statements and allegations were made concerning the location of the airport and its relationship to bird flyways in this area. In particular, it was stated that the effect of birds on the operation of the airport had not been considered adequately and that they would pose a serious hazard to safe flight operations. Assessment of this factor had in fact been made during the site selection process. However, it was subsequently felt that a much more detailed analysis was required in view of the allegations made by residents of the area. Accordingly, the Ministry of Transport engaged a well qualified environmental research firm to do a detailed ornithological study and we assume that this is the study in question. The study commenced in September of 1972 and will conclude in December of this year. This length of time was required in order that a detailed analysis of nesting habits, diurnal flight patterns and seasonal migration statistics could be assembled. The total cost of the study by the firm of LGL (Environmental Research Associates) Limited will be approximately $253,000. The results to date tend to confirm that the probability of bird hazards affecting aircraft operations in the area of the proposed airport is typical of that which might be expected in this part of southern Ontario and that no undue hazards will be presented. The study is, however, continuing in order to assess the fall migration period.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, October 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-164, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973 to the 30th day of June, 1974, and securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railways Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the House recessed for the weekend on Friday, I started to participate in a debate on Bill C-164 on financing the Canadian National Railways. I was commenting on the importance of transportation in areas such as Saskatchewan, in view of our farm population and innumerable small communities. I also stated that in Melville we have a large CNR terminal.
We on the prairies sometimes get very angry with Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway because it is a fact that these two railways have been responsible for some of the lack of development, high freight rates and discrimination against the prairies. I gave some examples of this in the debate last Friday. This afternoon, I want to spend a few minutes going over the immense power of CNR and CPR to show how these huge corporations affect the lives of people living in the prairies and, indeed, right across Canada.
What is the difference between CNR and CPR? I suggest they are basically the same type of beast. They just have different hides. CNR is publicly owned. CPR is a privately owned corporation. CPR operates in eight provinces, CNR in 10. CPR has a highway transportation organization. CNR has a highway transportation organization as well. CPR has coastal steamships. CNR has coastal steamships. Both have hotels. Both have a telecommunications company and network. Both are involved in the air transportation business. Both are involved in pipeline research in this country. Both are involved in tax ripoffs from the Canadian people.
In my own province, the Hotel Saskatchewan in Regina just last year started paying taxes to the city of Regina. Last year they paid $350,000 in taxes. That will be their annual tax rate from last year on. However, prior to that, the Hotel Saskatchewan did not pay any taxes at all, despite the fact it is owned by the CPR and has been in operation for many years. The city of Regina still pays the complete water bill for that huge hotel. In other words, these two rail lines have a virtual monopoly on the rail, air and water transportation in this country. Because of that, they exercise considerable control over national policy across this country.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
I want to go back in history for a few moments and express my concern about the monopoly grip these companies have on Canadian life. I urge the government to take the initiative when it comes to freight rates and national transportation policy. The CPR was started in 1880 when they were given some $25 million by the federal government. At that time they were also given 25 million acres of land, the site of which they could choose over the next 20-year period for their roadbeds, for their stations, docks, workshops, sheds and so on, which went along with their rail transport system. They were given tax exemptions by all three levels of government on everything connected with the railway system. They had tax exemptions on the lands which were given to them for the 20-year period after that land was obtained. The federal government itself built 700 miles of railway during that period, the cost of which, including the land, was some $140 million, and which today would be worth considerably more than that. The CPR was also given exclusive mineral rights as well as all kinds of land.
You may wonder why the CPR at that time was given such huge welfare cheques or hand-outs by the federal government of the time. There were 40 MPs in the House and 12 Senators, and on checking the records I find that many, if not most, of these MPs and Senators had an interest in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and were thus serving their self-interest by giving huge handouts to the CPR. The government also guaranteed, very interestingly at that time, the shareholders of the CPR that freight rates would be kept high enough so that there would be a minimum profit of 10 per cent on the capital invested in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. In 1897 the Crowsnest Pass agreement subsidized the building of the CPR into southeastern British Columbia. So that gives you a bit of the background of the Canadian Pacific Railway in this country which was started by rugged individualists by the use of huge handouts and concessions from the federal Conservative government of the day, in mineral rights, taxation, direct subsidies and so on right down the line.
Now, what has the CPR become today? Is it exclusively a railway company? It certainly is not, Mr. Speaker. I have been able to tabulate some of the interests the CPR has, and I am sure this will be of interest to the House as an example of transportation in Canada. The Canadian Pacific Oil and Gas people have petroleum rights in over 23 million acres of land in western Canada. Canadian Pacific Railway Hotels, which is part of Canadian Pacific investment along with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, owns and operates 11 hotels across this country. Marathon Realties owns a monstrous $310 million worth of assets and the $35 million Place du Canada in Montreal. Comin-co, which was formerly the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, owns or controls National Hardware Specialties Limited in Ontario, which is a zinc die-casting plant. Western Steel Limited is owned and controlled by the CPR in Vancouver. Another company the CPR owns is Pinepoint Mines Limited in Trail, B.C. They own Pacific Coast Terminals Limited in New Westminster. They own Ricken Mines in Yellowknife. They own Coast Copper in
7308

October 29, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada Trail, B.C. They own Sunco Mines Limited, which is also a copper mine.
The Canadian Pacific Railway, has interests in the United States. There is a zinc interest in the country of India. It has fertilizer, lead and electronic plants in the United States, and a lead smelting plant in Japan. There are Canadian fertilizer plants. There are six hydro-electric power plants in the Province of British Columbia and some pipeline interests as well. The CPR, with its fully-owned Canadian subsidiaries, had a net income last year of close to $70 million; Cominco, which is owned 53 per cent by the CP Investments Limited, has a net income of over $35 million; Pinepoint Mines Limited, which is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's as well, had a profit of over $35 million. These are some of the interests which Canadian Pacific Railway has and which show how it has become a huge monstrosity in the last few years in this country. And the CNR is not far behind the Canadian Pacific Railway when it comes to a corporate octopus with immense power in this country as well. In fact, Mr. Speaker, when I go back over some of the reports of the CPR I see that from 1920 their net profits have been $1,279 million. That indeed is immense and that, indeed, makes the company very, very powerful.
Now, Canadian National Railways has a very similar history. It is involved, as I say, in very similar enterprises across this country. Canadian National was formed by the amalgamation of several railways after 1920, railway companies that went broke, railway companies that a Conservative government again at that time bought out, fully compensating the owners thereof. The Canadian government guaranteed bonds of the Canadian National Railways to the tune of $860 million. This does not include the forgiveness of debt which occurred in 1937. It does not include the converted half of the $760 million debt which existed in 1952 in the form of preferred equity shares, and this does not include the forgiveness of interest for ten years, ending in 1961, of $100 million. Despite that, the debt I am told is still almost $2 billion.
Now the CNR, like the CPR, is also involved in all kinds of enterprises across the country. We have the railway system itself. We have CN Express. We have Canadian National Railways Limited in France. We have Canadian National Realties, Canadian National Steamship Company, Canadian National Telegraph, Canadian National Transfer, Canadian National Transportation. We have Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company, which is owned bh the CNR. We have Chapman Transportation Company, which is owned by the CNR; Eastern Transport, Empire Freightways, the Great Northwest Telegraph Company of Canada. We have Husband Transport, Husband International Transport, Midland Superior Enterprise Limited, the Minnesota-Manitoba Railroad Company, Minnesota-Ontario Bridge Company, Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company, all owned by the CNR.
I could go on and on listing the companies that are owned by the huge Canadian National Railways Company here and beyond our border. They own the Northern Consolidated Holding Company, Provincial Tankers Limited, the Quebec and Saint John Railway Company, Royal Transportation Limited, Scobe's Transport, Swan River-The Pas Transfer, Toronto-Peterborough Transportation

Company, Central Vermont Railway, which is operated, of course, in the United States, the Duluth-Rainy Lake and Winnipeg Railway in the Duluth and Winnipeg area, and so on. These are the companies that are run by the Canadian National Railways here in this country.
If we look back at the history of the CNR in this country we find they have been much more willing to provide aid and service to industrial developments than they have to the ordinary citizen through decent transportation service, passenger service and working conditions for the employees. We find that in 1952, the CNR and the government of Canada combined to offer great incentives to build a railway to Kitimat and a bridge across the Skeena river for mining industries in that area. The same thing happened with the Lynn Lake developments in Manitoba where the CNR and the government of Canada combined to build a railway called the Sherritt Gordon line.
So you can see as you go back through the history of the CNR that they have been very, very quick to use the taxpayers money to build services for some of the private mining companies and private interests in this country. And now we get down to 1973. What do we see the CNR trying to do in conjunction with the CPR in this country? Members hear about the terrible passenger service, about Air Canada, among other things, and I want to mention one or two more specific items relating to the prairies. We find now applications before the Canadian Transport Commission to abandon 3,000 miles of railway track in the Province of Saskatchewan alone. And this is in addition to the elimination of station agents during the last few years.
Why do they want to abandon railway tracks when they have this immense empire behind them which has made enormous profits over the last dozens of years? There are a number of reasons why they want to abandon railway lines on the prairies. First of all, the National Transportation Act provides that in order to qualify for subsidy a railway must first apply to abandon the lines in question. This is one of the reasons the railways have applied to abandon 3,000 miles of railway line in my province.
The CPR and CNR have both said that one reason they must abandon certain lines is competition from trucking companies, which is becoming so severe that they are losing money. But, Mr. Speaker, who owns a lot of the trucking companies in Canada? The CNR and CPR. What we have is their rail operation competing against their highway transport operation, and this is used as another excuse to abandon rail lines in my province. The railways also wanted to abandon grain elevators, but the farm organizations are disputing that kind of application. What they are really trying to do is maximize their profits because the rail lines serving these small towns are not returning to them a very high profit, certainly not the profit they would like to see.
I ask, why not use the port of Churchill more than we do to export grain from the prairies? This would save the farmers 10 to 15 cents a bushel because Churchill is closer to the prairies. But the railways refuse to do so, because when grain is shipped through the Lakehead and down the St. Lawrence seaway system the CPR and CNR

receive more revenue through freight rates than they would if grain were shipped through Churchill.
Another reason the railways want to abandon lines is that it costs about $35,000 per mile per year to keep the track in shape. This figure relates to railway lines all across the country, not necessarily to the specific ones they are trying to abandon. There are 3,000 miles of track in my province of Saskatchewan, which works out to a figure of $105 million a year for maintenance. In other words, they want to save $105 million a year in my province alone. Where would the saving go, Mr. Speaker? I am sure _ it would not go to the farmers in the form of increased assistance, because they would have to haul their grain much greater distances from the farm to the elevator terminal. I am sure the saving would go into the general treasuries of the two railways concerned. If the $105 million a year which would be saved in Saskatchewan if the railways' attempts to abandon the rail lines were successful were invested at a reasonable rate of return over a period of 20 years, it would produce some $4 billion, to say nothing of similar savings in other provinces in Canada if rail lines were abandoned.
Then, of course, there are other costs incurred by rail line abandonment. For example, what would happen to people in small towns, villages and hamlets if local grain elevators were closed down? This represents about half of their economic base, and therefore they would be unable to exist. The municipalities will lose a lot of their tax revenue, services would become more centralized, people would be encouraged to leave the areas and go to larger centres in order to seek jobs, bring up their families and even retire there. I suggest this is a serious issue. Before the minister allows the CTC to grant the applications to abandon these lines, the minister should understand not only the economic consequences of such an act but also the social consequences for the people in rural Saskatchewan, and others living in different parts of rural Canada similarly affected.
The government of Saskatchewan has stated that rail line abandonment should be postponed in this country until at least 1980. I urge the minister to listen to what the government of Saskatchewan has said since they, like other governments on the prairies, know what their people living in rural areas want. If that were the case, better services would be provided to these people and they would have a better way of life. The very set-up of the board of directors of our two railways militates against the interests of people on the prairies. For example, of the 24 members of the board of directors of the CPR, only three come from western Canada, 19 come from eastern Canada, and there are three from foreign countries. There are 14 directors of the CNR; only four come from the west and 10 from eastern Canada.
In a debate of this sort, I and other members from the prairie provinces want to take the opportunity to put forward the argument that our transportation system be used to the benefit of all people in this country, not just those who happen to be fortunate enough to live within the golden horseshoe of southern Ontario in and around the city of Toronto. The freight rate structure in Canada should be organized in such a way as to remove any anomalies. For example, unprocessed goods can be shipped
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada from Saskatchewan more cheaply than finished goods. This should not be the case, but as long as it is the case rural Saskatchewan will remain undeveloped, as will our north, most parts of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.
I would encourage the minister, in all seriousness, to inform the railways that they will not be allowed to abandon their rail lines. In addition, I suggest he remove freight rate anomalies and thus serve all of the people in this country. One way to do this would be to nationalize the CPR and run just one railway system in this country. With regard to compensation for the CPR, according to the ledgers that I have seen it would not cost much to buy out the CPR, because most of that empire was built with the taxpayers' money in the first place. They have been getting welfare cheques from us for years. It is now time that the people of Canada owned, operated and controlled that particular railway along with the CNR. Let us have one railway system in this country that will serve all of our people from coast to coast.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand there is one, possibly two, more speakers to follow me. It is not my intention to take up too much time, but there are one or two points I should like to bring forward in this debate.
Bill C-164, which we are presently debating, gives the members of this House an opportunity to discuss the many transportation problems we have in Canada. Having listened to the debate over the past few days, I find a number of very interesting proposals have been put forward by members of all parties which I trust will be given very careful consideration both by the Department of Transport and by the committee that will deal with the bill once we give it second reading.
I welcome the opportunity to raise several transportation problems in my riding of Kootenay West. As hon. members know, a number of members have spoken on pension matters, abandonment of railway lines and so on. Similar problems exist in other parts of Canada, and I think all arise because of the fact that the transportation policy of this nation is inadequate. It is the lack of a unified transportation policy that has led to much of our current difficulties on our transportation system in Canada. I feel that the lack of adequate national policy in this field can have disastrous results, particularly on the growth of certain areas. Coming from a rural area I find that sometimes these weak transportation policies can seriously harm the potential economic growth of those rural areas in which we are very interested in seeing jobs retained. Certain economic ventures, too, are often destroyed when rail lines are abandoned.
Canada is a country whose economy is dependent on vast amounts of both exports and imports. Large quantities of raw materials are to be found in every part of our nation, and fast and efficient transportation facilities are required to get these products to market so we can be competitive. In addition, we find that Canadians travel a great deal. Whether they are commuting to and from places of employment or travelling for business or pleasure, we find that some method of transport comes into the picture. Our country, with its huge area and vast dis-

Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
tances, uses many modes of transportation including rail, air, ship and, of course, our ever increasing truck transport. It is essential that all these methods be welded into a closely coordinated system to ensure that we receive the fast and efficient movement of goods and people that is required in this day and age. There is no reason all aspects of such a transport system should not be fully coordinated, owned and controlled by Canadians. It is for this reason the members of our group have been pressing for years for a Canadian merchant marine. I am not going to go into this because other members have spoken about the need for a Canadian merchant marine, but it does seem odd that Canada, a country with the longest coastline in the world, should have practically all its shipping trade carried in ships of other nations.
There are several transportation problems, however, which affect that part of B.C. I represent and to which attention must be paid to prevent further deterioration of transport facilities in the area. I should like to deal first with a problem which has been settled by the present B.C. government, but which could become a problem at some future date unless some legislative changes are made to prevent it. I refer to the recent plan to build the Kootenay and Elk railway to connect with the Burlington Northern at the United States border for the purpose of hauling coal from the east Kootenay to the Pacific coast via a United States railway line.
I firmly believe that Canadian raw materials and goods should be transported, wherever possible, by our own Canadian transportation systems, and as a result I welcomed, as did most residents of British Columbia, the action of the present B.C. government in stopping the export of Canadian jobs by the proposed plan to haul Canadian export coal over U.S. rail lines. The point I should like to make here is that the application to build the Kootenay and Elk railway should never have been allowed in the first place. This railway was only an appendage of a U.S. rail line and was to have no rolling stock of its own. Despite this, the lack of adequate federal legislation allowed the Kootenay and Elk to be incorporated under provincial law, although it was in no sense a provincial railway. This indicates that a legislative change is required in our Railway Act, and I urge the minister to proceed with it at an early date.
I might point out in passing that there are a number of products that various companies might be interested in having hauled over competing U.S. rail lines. I think legislation should be updated to make certain that appendages of U.S. rail lines cannot come into Canada and take away some of this lucrative rail freight haul. The former Social Credit government of British Columbia encouraged the building of the Kootenay and Elk railway. It would have meant the loss of many hundreds of Canadian railway jobs and would have been a severe blow to the Canadian economy. Their argument was, however, that it would provide competition for the CPR and, more important, it would provide an alternate route to the Pacific coast to ensure that our coal export contracts with Japan would not be placed in jeopardy. I might point out that there is already an alternative route to the Pacific coast and it is one which lies entirely within our own country. I refer to the Kettle Valley Line which more or less parallels the United States border. It runs from the East Koote-

nay area and now joins the main line of the CPR as it comes down the Fraser Canyon.
I believe there is a need for an alternate route to the Pacific coast from eastern B.C., but it should be confined to Canadian territory and, in my opinion, the Kettle Valley route would make an excellent alternative. It would relieve the growing pressure on the main line of the CPR and could be the safety valve in the event of a long and serious tie-up on this main line. It appears, however, that the company is reluctant to spend the necessary funds to make this line a viable alternative. It has reduced services and diverted traffic elsewhere in the hope, I presume, that eventually it will be able to persuade the Canadian Transport Commission that portions of the line should be abandoned. I would urge that a major upgrading of the Kettle Valley line take place. For a start it could be used to assist in the lucrative coal haul, perhaps by being used as the route to return the empty coal trains to east Kootenay, thus relieving some of the pressure now on the CPR main line.
At one time the Kettle Valley line went through the Coquahala Pass which gave it access to the Fraser Valley without having to go through the dangerous Fraser Canyon. This particular pass was abandoned a number of years ago by the CPR and, as a consequent result, all the rail traffic to the lower mainland, both CPR and CNR, must go down the Fraser Canyon. We can still vividly recall the immense traffic tie-up in the Fraser Canyon from the heavy snowfall of two years ago in which both our two transcontinental rail lines were involved. I understand there is a feasible route to get rail traffic into the Fraser Valley to the west of the dangerous Fraser Canyon. This matter should be investigated and, if found feasible, should be advocated by our National Transport Commission. Our increasing dependence upon continuous supplies of goods both to and from our Pacific seaboard is becoming of increasing significance as time goes on.
Many members during this debate have mentioned the economic upset and trouble which will be caused by the proposed abandonment policies of both our national rail lines. I find the same situation arises in my constituency of Kootenay West, where rail lines have been abandoned by the CPR, and the company is making moves to abandon more of its small branch lines. I might add that once a rail line has been removed from the area the chance of economic development taking place is greatly reduced. Once the rail line goes, we see a considerable number of small economic job-producing enterprises go with it, and as a result these little communities become less attractive because of a decreased number of job opportunities. There has been talk of diversification of industry throughout our country in an attempt to cut down on many of the major problems which now confront us with a growing concentration of citizens in urban areas. Unfortunately, the transportation policy of the present government has done nothing to ensure the continuity and growth of our smaller rural centres and is leading to increased urbanization as time goes on.
I understand that in 1975 the CPR will try to abandon the rail link between Rosebery and Nakusp. The company would very much like to get rid of this phase of its operation. Over the years there has been a gradual erosion
October 29, 1973

of service by the company in this area, and this is no doubt directed toward the final abandonment of service to the area. It is my intention to oppose any further abandonment of rail lines in Kootenay West. The entire area has tremendous economic potential and this will gradually be developed over the next few years. We must not allow the CPR, with its faulty transportation theories, to slow down or stop the type of economic development which should and could be taking place in British Columbia.
This is the reason so many members have stressed the need for Canada to make some major changes in this whole policy in respect of transportation and communication. This bill deals with Air Canada and with air service in general. I should like to speak very briefly on air communication service in and out of Kootenay West. It should and could be improved. For example, in this day and age we find there is not a daily service from Castlegar airport to Calgary and the east. This just does not make sense. Pacific Western Airlines, which has the franchise for the area, should be obliged to institute a daily service. Once travellers are certain a daily service is available this helps generate passenger travel. It is disconcerting to air travellers to be forced on certain days to either stay overnight in Calgary or fly to Vancouver and then return several hundred miles to Castlegar. The additional cost involved is an unfair levy on those travellers who are forced to take the Vancouver route.
Another aspect of air communication which requires more attention is the growing need for improvement to existing municipal air fields and the development of new ones. This is an area of communication which is showing rapid development and one which needs far more attention than it has received to date. Rapid communication within a region is essential, for many centres are a long distance from those airports which are serviced by a licensed airline. Facilities are required to ensure that charter flights can provide services if required. There is also a rapidly growing use of private planes for both business and pleasure. This phase of air travel also needs attention, and I would urge the Department of Transport to allocate far more funds to the development of facilities for this type of air travel.
There are some immediate requirements in my area for improved service in this field. Every existing airport needs improvements. The priority in this regard is certainly at the Trail municipal airport at Columbia Gardens where the immediate need is for a paved runway. The department is aware of the problems, and I will press the government to see that action is taken on them.
There are a host of other problems, but this is second reading of this particular bill. Most members have covered other aspects of transportation and when this bill comes back to the House for report stage it is my intention to again raise several of the points I have briefly mentioned here this afternoon and to suggest other points I should like to question the minister about. I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words and trust that some time today this bill will receive second reading in the House.

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN (No. 2) AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ANNUAL INCREASES AND LEVEL OF INCOME ON WHICH CONTRIBUTIONS BE PAID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue the point of order of which I gave notice on Tuesday, October 23, as recorded in Hansard at pages 7136 and 7137.1 realize that it is rather unusual for a member to raise a point of order with respect to a bill the terms of which he fully supports. Nevertheless, rules are rules and should be held in high regard. I also feel that there are certain consequences from the point I wish to make which should be considered, indeed certain rights which should be preserved. The point of order that I raise has to do with the fact that when this bill was placed on the order paper and given first reading there was attached to it what we call the royal recommendation. That recommendation, which is given by His Excellency the Governor General, is required in all cases where a bill involves the expenditure of public money or, to put it in other terms, in all cases where any money has to be paid out of or charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
It is my contention, and I think it is so well supported it hardly needs to be argued, that that is not true with respect to the Canada Pension Plan. It is a completely self sustaining plan. In fact, its self sustaining character is so
Canada Pension Plan (No. 2) complete that even charges for rent, telephone and all other kinds of administrative services are made against the plan or against the fund which is set up under the Canada Pension Plan.
The Canada Pension Plan was first brought in 1964 but it was passed in 1965. At that time there was a resolution that preceded the bill. This was before the days when we had abolished the resolution, but it took the same form as the Governor General's recommendation now takes. Some questions were asked about this at that time. The answer given by the then Prime Minister, the late Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, was to the effect that when the plan got operating it would of course be completely self-sustaining, but to begin with there were certain costs involved in getting the plan established, certain expenditures that had to be made before any receipts came in, and that in that sense there were initial charges that had to be paid by the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
However, one of the requirements of the original act, the Canada Pension Plan as passed in 1965, was that any of these costs that had been incurred before the plan came into effect were to be paid back to the Consolidated Revenue Fund out of the fund established under the Canada Pension Plan. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because the Canada Pension Plan as it now operates is a plan which does not draw on the Consolidated Revenue Fund in any way, it seems to me that it is an act of supererogation or, to put it in simple language, it is wrong to attach a Governor General's recommendation to this amending bill. Someone might say, "No harm is done. Let's be on the safe side." But of course the harm that is done is that if the Chair rules that such a recommendation is required then private members are denied the right to make any amendments, even though their amendments might not require any payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
With regard to the fact that no charges are made against the Consolidated Revenue Fund may I remind hon. members that if they look at the public accounts of Canada from year to year they will see that there is an account known as the Canada Pension Plan account, but it is completely separated from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Also it will be noted that some of the expenditures that are listed as charged to the Canada Pension Plan are administrative costs, rental of space and all the rest of it. In other words, the principle that everything must be paid for out of the contributions that employers and employees pay into the Canada Pension fund is well protected. Indeed this is guaranteed in section 110 of the Canada Pension Plan itself, which is found at page 849 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970, vol. 1. It fills a column so I will not read it in full, but it does say very clearly that everything that is received by way of Canada Pension Plan contributions must go into the Canada Pension Plan account, and every payment that is made out with respect to the Canada Pension Plan must be charged to the Canada Pension Plan account.
Then, there is subsection (4) of section 110 which says:
No payment shall be made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund under this section in excess of the amount of the balance to the credit of the Canada Pension Plan Account.

October 29, 1973
Canada Pension Plan (No. 2)
In other words, it is very clear that not one cent can go out of the federal treasury, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, for the payment of any of the costs of the Canada Pension Plan, whether it be the paying of pensions or other benefits or whether it be the paying of administrative costs. This has been argued a number of times. It seems to me that the arguments that took place in 1964 and 1965 on this point were not really conclusive, because there was a mixed bag at that time, but since then the expenses involved in getting the plan going and any expenses that were paid prior to the starting of the plan, have been paid back.
A more recent discussion of this point is one that took place on April 20, 1971. I am looking at a number of pages in Hansard for that day, pages 5093 to 5097. I may say at the outset that I find it interesting in addressing you, Sir, as Mr. Speaker, that two of the persons who took part in the debate that day were a predecessor of yours, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), and the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants, who is now the occupant with you of what he calls that lonely plateau.
Since both of these esteemed gentlemen, one a former speaker and the other the present Deputy Speaker, made statements about the matter I think it will be interesting to have Your Honour's view on the matter as well. When I first looked at these pages I thought that maybe my quoting of these two gentlemen would be offset by the fact that you said something that day. But no, Sir, you were not in the chair that day. It was Mr. Honey, deputy speaker in the last parliament who was in the chair. So, Sir, this is your golden opportunity. You have not ruled on this point yet, and you have such excellent authorities as the hon. member for Edmonton West, a former occupant of the chair, and your present colleague, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave).
On that occasion the bill being discussed was a private member's bill which had been presented by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and the arguments I have given today in brief were given then by all of us who took part on the side of private member's rights. In the end Mr. Honey ruled against us, but I draw attention to the fact that he based his ruling almost exclusively on the fact that Bill C-34 in that session, a bill in which the hon. member for Hillsborough sought to amend the Canada Pension Plan in a certain way, did include a clause which said:
Expenditures under this Act shall be provided under section 104 of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1970.
There was that element of weakness in the bill that was before the House on that day. But, Mr. Speaker, I point out that there is not one jot or one tittle in Bill C-224 now before us that says anything shall be paid as provided under section 104 of the British North America Acts, 1867-1970. In fact Bill C-224 does not touch at all the sacred provision of section 110 of the Canada Pension Plan Act which says that not one red cent-I will come back to that phrase in a moment-shall be paid out of the federal treasury for the purposes of the Canada Pension Plan. Therefore it seems to me that this bill is not a money bill in the normal sense and that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), in whose name it is,

should be able to proceed with it without the royal recommendation.
Let it be quite clear that one of my motives in raising this matter is that I want to protect rights that I think we have as private members. Once this bill is before us of course the Canada Pension Plan is open, and I think we should have the right to make suggestions, and even to move amendments that would make improvements in the Canada Pension Plan if we can demonstrate that this can be done without involving any charge on the treasury.
I realize that any such amendments which we might make would have to be considered when they would come along, but of course we are locked outside to begin with if it is ruled that this is a money bill and that there has to be a royal recommendation, because then we are faced with the citation that says that the royal recommendation lays down once and for all the terms of the bill.
I said earlier that we had an interesting debate on April 20, 1971. I should like to quote a few words from one of the authorities who spoke that day. In the present context he is probably the one whom we should most like to quote. As recorded at page 5095 of Hansard for April 20, 1971, the hon. member said:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join briefly in the arguments that have been presented to Your Honour and to recall some of the wording in the resolution that was presented to the House when the Canada Pension Plan was introduced on October 28, 1964. But before I read portions of the resolution, I agree that up to that point the moneys had been spent by government departments with reference to the setting up of the plan, particularly with reference to the studies that had preceded the setting up of the plan, in that very special sense, involved an expenditure of tax moneys, of Her Majesty's revenues, in relation to that legislation. These moneys had to be spent so that the expertise established for publication of these ideas could be incorporated into the Canada Pension Plan itself.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has recalled, the then member for Rosthern raised with the prime minister of the day the question of why there should be a resolution when the Canada Pension Plan was to pay its own expenses. There were exchanges between them, and perhaps I should read what the prime minister said then:
The hon. member then quotes Mr. Pearson as follows:
The fact is that it will cost some money to get this plan into operation, as my hon. friend must know. Afterwards, when the plan is in operation, the expenses will be borne by the fund.
It is no secret that the person whose words I am quoting, as recorded in Hansard of April 20, 1971, is the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants. He went on, from that basis, to argue that the resolution as attached to the original Canada Pension Plan bill was there purely for technical reasons but, now that the plan is paying its own way, it should be possible for a private member to move amendments to the legislation. As the hon. member pointed out, no money was to come out of the federal treasury.
I alluded awhile ago to "not one red cent" coming out of the federal treasury. Of course, I was in part repeating what the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants had said. Discussing the bill on that occasion and pointing out that it did not involve any charge on the treasury, the hon. member put it this way:
When could there be any requirement whatsoever that so much as

Canada Pension Plan (No. 2) was then the minister of national revenue. He did not wish to become involved in that debate because, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said and as the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), as he then was, said, there was not one jot or tittle of evidence within Bill C-5, then under consideration, to support the authorization of the payment of one red cent out of the fund. May I say that the ruling on the matter that precipated the debate on April 20, 1971 was, as I have said before, erroneous. Having reread all the material referred to and the debate of April 20, I am still convinced that the original ruling was erroneous and should not be followed.
First, if the royal recommendation is to be carefully and scrupulously followed by the Chair, as Mr. Deputy Speaker suggested the other day, there is a corresponding obligation to make sure that the recommendation is required. Second, there is the obligation to make sure that the recommendation is couched in correct terms. I say that because it cannot be used, shall we say, to stand off private members. If it is included for that reason, I suggest it is not proper. I suggest that this is what we are debating today.
I put it to Your Honour that there is no need for a recommendation in this particular case, as the bill seeks a change in the distribution of funds paid into the Canada Pension Plan by the contributors. From that plan the government of Canada cannot derive one cent for ways and means, and it cannot spend one cent for administration. The late Prime Minister Pearson remarked at one stage there would not be any money required to get the program in operation. The money was not paid back from the sources. The money was provided under item L60(b) in an appropriation bill which was passed and received royal assent as Bill C-150 of 1964-65. The Canada Pension Plan Act went through as Bill C-151.
In the revision of the statutes in 1970-71, if one looks to the historical index of what happened to all appropriations, we still see that opposite L60(b) is marked "spent". Therefore, the whole of that appropriation has gone. It is cleaned out. The loan has been repaid. Here is a little known fact. The government derived more money, and attempted to get even more money out of the fund, than it had spent with regard to the expenses of getting the plan geared up and under way.
An attempt was made to collect the expenses of public servants who had devoted time, travel and expenses in the 1950's in connection with the establishment of the Canada Pension Plan. The government of Canada tried to reimburse itself from a fund that belonged to the citizens of Canada. However, it was determined that until there was an amendment to the Canadian constitution in 1964 authorizing and permitting the government of Canada to get into a Canada Pension Plan, there was no authority to recover any moneys. The recovery of the so-called expenditures was stopped as of 1964.
That is an aside, but it indicates that the government of Canada cannot use any of the moneys under this plan for general purposes under the consolidated revenue fund. In any event, all of the expenses of organization and so forth

October 29, 1973
Canada Pension Plan (No. 2) have long since been repaid and there are funds far in excess of the requirements of the plan. It is argued that the citizens of Canada are being shortchanged by reason of the fact that loans made from the Canada Pension Plan fund are at a much lower rate of interest than the market. Therefore, the fund could provide moneys for the payment of the increase that is now being asked if the current interest rates were being charged. There would be sufficient moneys to make these payments. There would be no difficulty.
Many arguments could be made, but I come back to what I think bothers most members. In particular, it bothered Deputy Speaker Honey in 1971 when he considered that if it was not a tax, it was an impost. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the impost arises out of an old method of classifying or drawing up taxation statutes.
Prior to 1830, taxing statutes provided for the purpose for which the money was to be used. There were, therefore, limitations on the expenditures. For example, if a particular bill imposed a tax on tobacco for health purposes, the total amount of that tax had to be used for health purposes and no other purpose. It was in 1830 that the consolidated revenue fund was established by the United Kingdom government of the day. Therefore, we have a consolidated revenue fund into which all taxes are paid. Taxes are generally exacted under the Income Tax Act, the Customs Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act.
This left parliament free to exact a statute that dealt solely with the purpose for which the expenditure was to be made and, instead of including a tax, provide only that a certain sum was to be paid out of the consolidated fund either in the statute itself or in a subsequent appropriation act. The old method is still, but rarely, used. The Old Age Security Act is a classic example of an impost because it provides that a proportion of the expenditures were to be provided by an additional 2 per cent sales tax.
If Deputy Speaker Honey was right in his ruling on April 20, 1971, then the provisions of the Standing Orders relating to Ways and Means apply. A Ways and Means motion must be tabled under Standing Order 60(1) and, if adopted, a bill then brought in based on the provisions of such motion. The bill now before the House must be ruled out of order as not complying with Standing Order 60.
That is the dilemma that comes about from considering the contributions and the whole scheme of payments under the Canada Pension Plan Act as being part of a tax or an impost. Our Standing Orders and Section 54 of the BNA Act say we must proceed via another way if this is a tax, but this is not the way. This act is then bad. On the other hand, if this act is to be right, there cannot be any Ways and Means application. There cannot be any question of a tax or impost. Therefore, the recommendation is unnecessary. If the recommendation is unnecessary, the bill is then amendable. That, in essence, is the nub of the problem facing Your Honour at the present time.
I repeat what was said on March 12 as it appears at page 12290 of Hansard and subsequent pages.

This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the House by a message from the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.

Surely, the funds involved here are not only part of the revenue of the federal government, but go back to the provinces; they are used, for example, by local school boards and I submit they are part of public revenue. It has been argued, apparently, that these funds are not paid out of consolidated revenue. Surely, they are. It is said they come from the Canada Pension Plan fund, a fund in which money must always be available in order that applications for payment may be met. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that what are involved here are not only payments from the Consolidated Revenue Fund but payments by the federal government into the Canada Pension Plan fund on behalf of the 250,000 or 275,000 employees of the federal government. This contribution represents a direct expenditure on the part of the government and for this reason a recommendation by the Governor General is needed. I have no idea how many millions of dollars these contributions will amount to, but the total sum is bound to be a very large one.
It seems to me the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) really tipped his hand when he said he and his friends wanted to see this done without a recommendation in order that in private members hour they could bring in bills to amend the Canada Pension Plan.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN (No. 2) AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ANNUAL INCREASES AND LEVEL OF INCOME ON WHICH CONTRIBUTIONS BE PAID
speechtext:
If there are no additional contributions to this very important and interesting procedural debate, I shall attempt to make a ruling. The hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) has suggested that he, and the hon. members who sit around him, consider this procedural matter very seriously, and I expect them to do so because it is an important procedural point. It was raised some days ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and it is in response to the caveat received from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the Chair undertook to make a thorough study of precedents and citations from learned authors to determine whether there was substance in the suggestion that the royal recommendation was not required in this particular case.
Hon. members appreciate the difficulty with which the Chair is faced. There is a long established principle at stake here, a principle which has been confirmed for
Canada Pension Plan (No. 2) many, many years, and in all instances, I may say, by Speakers who have preceded me. I hope hon. members will not expect the Chair to go into all those rulings. I have tried to come to what I consider to be the substance of the matter in order to reach a conclusion.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised this point in relation to Bill C-224 and to the royal recommendation, which reads as follows:
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House of Commons the present measure to amend the Canada Pension Plan to remove the limitation of two per cent in the annual increase in the pension index within the meaning of the Act, to fix the year's maximum pensionable earnings for 1974 at $6,000, for 1975 at $7,400, and to provide thereafter that increases in the consumer price index be fully reflected in the escalation of benefits payable under the Act.
Hon. members have suggested that there was no need for such a recommendation since, in their view, the expenditures which may result from the adoption of the bill would be paid out of the Canada Pension Account and would not be any charge on the treasury. This, at least, is the way I understood the argument which was suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he first broached this subject, and the three hon. members to my left who (spoke) pretty well followed this line.
I have carefully studied Bill C-224 and have listened attentively to the arguments which were put forward earlier this afternoon. As I understand it, Bill C-224 seeks to change the Canada Pension Plan by increasing the year's maximum pensionable earnings for 1974 and 1975. As a result of the amendments proposed, contributions by both employees and employers would be increased. The federal government itself is an employer, and consequently its contribution to the fund would be increased. I say this with great respect, since I have much admiration for the wisdom of the hon. members who have taken part in this debate, but it seems to me that this is perhaps an aspect of the matter that they have not touched upon, at least in detail. Section 119 of the Act provides that contributions to be made by the Crown as employers' contributions in respect of persons employed by the Crown shall be charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and credited to the Canada Pension Plan Account.
The suggestion that this constitutes a charge on the treasury finds support in a citation from Sir Erskine May's Parliamentary Procedure, 18th edition, page 745 which reads as follows:
The imposition of charges on funds, other than the Consolidated Fund or the National Loans Fund does not require the royal recommendation, unless it involves an increased payment out of those Funds, or increases the liability (e.g. through a guarantee) upon them, or automatically attracts a grant from moneys provided by Parliament. The National Insurance Fund and the National Insurance (Industrial Injuries) Fund are examples of this kind of fund; and proposals to increase the benefits payable out of them do not require the royal recommendation . ..
But any increase in exchequer contributions to these funds or in the expenses incurred in administering them-even though ultimately recoverable by the exchequer must, of course, be recommended by the Crown.
This is where I have some difficulty finding in favour of the arguments advanced by hon. members. They suggest

October 29, 1973
Canada Pension Plan (No. 2) that moneys paid out of the Canada Pension Plan account are not moneys paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Yet section 110, of the Canada Pension Plan Act to which hon. members have referred, clearly provides that there shall be established in the accounts of Canada an account to be known as the Canada Pension Plan Account; that there shall be paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund and credited to the Canada Pension Plan Account all amounts received under the Act as or on account of contributions or otherwise. Subsection (4) of section 110 provides:
No payment shall be made out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund under this section in excess of the amount of the balance to the credit of the Canada Pension Plan Account.
I fail to follow the argument proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who quoted section 110(4) as evidence that no moneys will be paid from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. It seems to confirm that all payments actually made and authorized under section 110(3) of the Act would have to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund in accordance with section 110(4).
May I also refer hon. members to Bourinot's Fourth Edition, page 417, which reads as follows:
Besides the grants voted in the estimates there are certain payments which have not been provided for annually, but are defrayed out of the consolidated fund in conformity with various statutes. These payments comprise: costs and charges incident to the collection and management of the revenue; interest of the public debt; salaries of governor-general, lieutenant-governors, judges, etc.; loans, grants to provinces under the Union Act; and all other permanent payments. Whenever it is necessary to make any changes with respect to these permanent grants, they must be introduced in the shape of resolutions in committee of the whole, and bills founded thereon.
It is a fact, of course, that the resolution stage of a bill containing charges on the public revenue is no longer part of our procedure, but the requirement of a recommendation of the Crown still forms a fundamental and essential part of our procedure. May I refer hon. members to section (2) of citation 246 of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, which reads as follows:
The Governor-General's recommendation to any resolution involving a payment out of the public treasury must be formally given by a privy councillor in his place at the very initiation of a proceeding, i.e., as soon as the motion has been proposed for the House to go into committee on the resolution.
All hon. members are familiar with the provisions of section (1) of Standing Order 62, to which hon. members have referred, which is based, of course, on the relevant section of the British North America Act.
Hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, have referred to private members' bills amending The Canada Pension Plan which either have been allowed or disallowed. I should like to refer in particular to a bill sponsored by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) which came forward on March 29, 1972. After due consideration this bill was given the benefit of the doubt and allowed to proceed, even though it was moved by a private meniber and was not accompanied by a recommendation. The bill provided that housewives might become part of the plan where they contributed both for the employee and the employer. With respect, that was quite a different proposition from the one now before us. In addition, the Chair did enter a caveat about the possi-

bility that the financial initiative of the Crown might be involved.
Hon. members have also referred to a bill which, I believe, was introduced by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) entitled "An Act to amend the Canada Pension Plan (Pension Index)", which by the way is another purpose of Bill C-224. This bill was ruled out of order on April 20, 1971 as infringing the financial initiative of the Crown. This and other precedents which were quoted for the guidance of the Chair were all instances where the amending bills were ruled out of order.
Hon. members have suggested that perhaps the time has come for the Speaker to overrule the former Deputy Speaker, and even to overrule himself, in relation to a decision which had been made in committee of the whole by the then Chairman, appealed to the Deputy Speaker in his capacity as Acting Speaker and confirmed by the Deputy Speaker in that capacity, and then confirmed by a vote of the House.
I suggest with great respect to hon. members that it is extremely difficult for the Chair to accept the suggestion that all these precedents should be disregarded and a different decision reached at the present time. I fully sympathize with hon. members regarding the ability of private members to introduce bills or to propose amendments, including amendments to the present act, but hon. members will appreciate and agree with me that the Chair is bound by precedents, particularly by the Standing Orders, which reflect the position proposed by the British North America Act, and by our practice and cutoms regarding the requirement when charges on the treasury are involved.
I am fully appreciative of the fact that I may not have dealt with all aspects of the arguments which were advanced, particularly the very interesting and forceful argument of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). But I doubt that the majority of hon. members would feel I would be justified in disregarding all the precedents and past practices of the House in reaching the conclusion that the royal prerogative in this case should be disregarded, that we should communicate with His Excellency and tell him that we would like to return his recommendation, that it is not needed and is superfluous in the present circumstances. Therefore, I must reach the conclusion that I should not entertain the point of order raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased this afternoon to launch the debate on Bill C-224. There are only a few minutes left before five o'clock and I hope I shall be able to go into details when the debate resumes later this evening.
Six months ago last Thursday, the government tabled its Working Paper on Social Security in Canada. This signalled the start of the joint federal-provincial review of Canada's total social security system that had been suggested by the government of Canada and the provinces.
October 29, 1973

Since this review began, legislation has been introduced to reform and substantially increase family and youth allowances in Canada.
Today, Bill C-224 deals with amendments to the Canada Pension Plan and we are about to debate it. It constitutes the third major piece of legislation the government is introducing as a product of this comprehensive review of Canada's social security system.
Shortly after I tabled the working paper of the federal government, I met with provincial Ministers of Welfare, and I conferred with them again two weeks ago on the reforms that should be made in the Canada Pension Plan. In the intervening period, federal and provincial welfare officials met on numerous occasions, and had jointly prepared a number of detailed studies to assist the ministers of welfare at their October meeting.
In addition, during this interval, I consulted with members of the Canada Pension Plan Advisory Committee, and representatives of labour and business organizations. The results of these extensive studies and consultations with the provinces and private organizations can be found in the communique which the provincial Ministers of Welfare and I issued on October 11, 1973 with respect to the agreements we had reached on the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you would allow me to review very briefly the principal areas of agreement between the provinces and the federal government that are outlined in the joint communique. The government of Canada and the provinces where the Canada Pension Plan operates, and the government of Quebec, where the Quebec Pension Plan operates, have agreed that legislation whould be introduced so that, first, starting in 1974, pensions paid under both the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans will be fully escalated in response to increases in the cost of living; second, the earnings ceiling for pension calculations, and contributions to both the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans will be $6,600 for 1974, and thereafter will be increased by 12 Vi per cent a year until the ceiling reaches the average earnings of Canadian industrial workers. At the present time, the earnings ceiling is $5,600 under the Canada Pension Plan, and $5,900 under the Quebec Pension Plan; third, the level of earnings exempted from Canada Pension Plan contributions will be $700 for 1974 and thereafter will be set, under both the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan, at 10 per cent of the earnings ceiling for Canada Pension Plan and Quebec Pension Plan contributions. At the present time, the level of exempt earnings is $600 under the Canada Pension Plan, and $700 under the Quebec Pension Plan; and, fourth, effective 1974, the earnings test which now applies to persons drawing CPP retirement pensions between the ages of 65 and 69 will be eliminated.
The federal and provincial governments also agreed that other issues which had been raised, in many quarters, in connection with the reform of the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans such as those relating to equality between men and women with regards to contributions and benefits, non-contributing spouses, early retirement provisions, and the level of survivors and disability benefits under the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans should receive priority attention.
Administration of Justice
These agreements, if enacted by the Parliament of Canada and the Quebec legislature, will have a profound effect on the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. They mean, among other things, that maximum CPP retirement pensions, which now run at about $90 a month, could reach a level of $250 a month by the end of this decade.

Let me explain at the outset that I am not committed to every phrase and nuance of the
